summary: TDDev automates acceptance-test generation from requirements, LLM-driven browser testing of the deployed app, and translation of failures into repair feedback, exposed as MCP tools (start_app/run_tests/stop_app). A controlled study on 20 WebGen-Bench apps compares Vanilla generation with three TDD loops (Incremental, Whole-Project, Agentic) across a minimal Claude-Agent-SDK agent and OpenCode with three backbones (Claude Sonnet 4.6, MiniMax-M3, Qwen3.5-397B), with paired Wilcoxon tests and bootstrap CIs.

claims.claim: With capable backbones TDD improves accuracy by 15.5–23.7 pp.
claims.evidence: Table 6 (Sonnet): Vanilla 67.8 → Incr 84.6 (+16.8***), Whole 83.2 (+15.5**), Agent 91.5 (+23.7***); Fig. 2 (MiniMax): +15.8 to +22.3 minimal agent, +16.7–17.1 OpenCode, p<.01. Numbers match abstract. Caveat: the oracle test cases are the same human-authored WebGen-Bench tests converted into acceptance tests and fed into the TDD loop (§4.5.2), while Vanilla does not see them — so part of the gain is test visibility, not TDD per se. One run per cell, n=20 apps.

claims.claim: TDD remains effective for both minimal and full-featured coding agents.
claims.evidence: Fig. 2: OpenCode Vanilla 72.0 → 88.8–89.2 with MiniMax; only one backbone tested on OpenCode.

claims.claim: Unreliable feedback negates TDD for weaker models; a stronger tester restores gains.
claims.evidence: Table 6: Qwen3.5 self-feedback −4.4 to +4.8 (n.s.); with Sonnet feedback +6.8 to +9.4 (p .056/.092/<.05). Table 7: failure-verdict rate 56.2% vs 21.3%, regression 47.6% vs 14.7%. Mechanism well-documented; significance marginal.

claims.claim: Whole-Project TDD is most cost-efficient in most configurations.
claims.evidence: Table 9: 4.97–10.33 pp per M additional tokens in 4 of 5 configs; 96.3% of build tokens are input.

claims.claim: TDDev's testing agent catches 100% of defects; test generation covers 88.9% of reference criteria.
claims.evidence: Table 5: 40 fixture evaluations on 10 hand-made micro-apps, 20/20 broken detected, 75% on correct apps (5 FPs). Table 4: 575/647 reference criteria, matched by an LLM (Claude) semantic judge without human validation of the matching.
Table 10: 3 developers × 2 sessions vs Bolt.diy; 0 vs 4.7 min manual time. Tiny convenience sample.

patterns.note: Acceptance-test-first loop raises oracle accuracy 15–24 pp for capable models; fails or hurts when the tester model is weak.
Deploy-and-exercise execution feedback loop drives repairs; quality of the verifier is the binding constraint.
Requirements turned into explicit, per-behavior acceptance tests that both guide and gate generation.
LLM browser tester used as both in-loop verifier and final oracle; 87.5% accuracy on 40 fixtures, false positives on correct apps; Qwen tester misattributes its own errors.
Packaging TDD tools as an MCP server let the same tools plug into two different agents (minimal agent, OpenCode) and Bolt.diy.
Human reviews proposed acceptance tests once, then loop runs unattended (user study).

methodology.sample: 20 apps randomly sampled (seed 42) from 101 WebGen-Bench tasks; RQ1 coverage on all 101; 40 fixture evaluations; 3-developer user study.
methodology.baselines: Vanilla single-pass generation per agent/backbone; Bolt.diy in user study. No non-TDD iterative-repair baseline that sees the same tests without TDD structure.
methodology.models: Claude Sonnet 4.6, MiniMax-M3, Qwen3.5-397B-A17B (temp 0, reasoning off); oracle tester fixed to Claude Sonnet 4.6.
methodology.variance: Paired one-sided Wilcoxon and 10k-resample bootstrap 95% CIs over apps; single run per app/condition.
methodology.ablations: Three TDD implementations × agents × backbones; feedback-model swap (Qwen dev + Sonnet tester).
methodology.languages: Full-stack web apps (JS/TS front ends with backends); no Java.

biases.detail: Oracle tests are the same tests given to the TDD loop; Vanilla never sees them, so TDD vs Vanilla conflates test-first workflow with test visibility.

Final oracle is an LLM browser tester (Claude Sonnet 4.6) validated only on 40 fixture checks; it is also the developer/tester in the Sonnet configuration (shared-model bias). Test coverage matched by an LLM semantic judge.
20 apps, one run per cell; 3-person user study.
No repeated runs to separate run-to-run nondeterminism from condition effects (CIs are across apps only).
WebGen-Bench apps are small greenfield web apps, not changes to existing multi-module backends.

verdict_reason: Peer-reviewed (ASE'26), factorial design across agents/backbones with significance tests and CIs, released code, and a useful negative result on weak testers. Caveats: the in-loop acceptance tests equal the oracle tests, the oracle is an LLM tester with modest validation, 20 small greenfield web apps, single runs.
applicability: Directly relevant to the team's spec-driven rollout: derive executable acceptance tests from the spec, have a human approve them, then let the agent loop against them — the paper shows this pays off only if the verifier is reliable. For a Java backend, the verifier should be deterministic (JUnit/REST-assured/contract tests against the ingestion and delivery APIs) rather than an LLM browser agent, which removes the paper's main weakness. Packaging start/test/stop as an MCP server is a host-neutral way to give the same loop to Cursor, Claude Code, Codex, etc. Whole-Project loops amortize context cost best. Does not address changes spanning ≥4 existing repos or healthcare content correctness; front-end delivery checks could reuse the browser-testing idea.
